questions.question: A team of five developers needs to release to production multiple times per day while keeping main green. Which branching strategy fits this requirement best in Azure Repos?
options: GitFlow with a permanent develop branch, version-specific release branches, and pull requests merged to both develop and main on every change
Forking workflow where each developer maintains a personal fork and a release manager periodically merges cross-repository pull requests upstream
Trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches merged to main via pull request, gated by a CI pipeline that blocks merges on test failure
Environment branches such as dev, staging, and prod where promotion happens by merging dev into staging and then staging into prod after a code review pass
questions.explanation: Trunk-based development with short-lived branches is the recommended pattern for continuous delivery: it minimises long-running divergence, keeps integration cost low, and pairs naturally with feature flags so partially complete work can ship safely. GitFlow's develop and release layers add a merge tax suited to scheduled releases, not many-times-per-day deployments. Forking workflows are designed for arms-length open-source contribution where contributors lack write access — a five-person internal team has no need for that overhead. Environment branches couple deployment promotion to merges, so a rollback or a hotfix has to walk the same merge ladder and parallel work becomes tangled.
questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy

questions.question: A pull request to main must be blocked until a CI build passes and at least one reviewer from the team approves. Which Azure Repos mechanism enforces both conditions natively?
options: A server-side Git pre-receive hook on the Azure DevOps repository that rejects pushes to main lacking an approved reviewer comment and a linked build status
A YAML pipeline configured with a pull request trigger that runs the validation build and reports its result back to the PR view for reviewers to see
A branch policy on main configuring required reviewers, a minimum approver count, and a build validation policy that runs a specified pipeline on every update
An Azure Function webhook that listens for pull-request events, queues the build pipeline, and adds a merge-allowed label after both checks succeed
questions.explanation: Branch policies on a protected branch are the native control. Required reviewers and a minimum approver count enforce human review, while a build validation policy runs the named pipeline on every PR update and blocks the merge until it succeeds. Azure DevOps does not expose user-configurable server-side Git hooks on hosted repositories, so the pre-receive option is not actually available to configure. A PR trigger only reports the build status onto the PR — it does not block the merge button by itself; the merge block comes from the branch policy that consumes that status. A custom Function webhook is a homegrown workaround that duplicates the built-in reviewer plus build validation policy and has no enforced merge gate of its own.
questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy

questions.question: An Azure Pipelines workflow must build an application, deploy it to a staging environment, then deploy it to production only after manual approval. What is the recommended way to model this end-to-end flow?
options: Two separate classic release pipelines that share build artifacts, with a manual approval gate added on the production pipeline
A single YAML pipeline using a runtime parameter deployToProd defaulting to false, where operators rerun the pipeline with the parameter flipped to true
Three independent YAML pipelines chained with pipeline resource triggers, where the production pipeline starts when the staging pipeline completes successfully
A single YAML pipeline containing build, staging, and production stages, with the production stage targeting an Environment resource that has approval checks
questions.explanation: Multi-stage YAML pipelines model build, staging, and production as separate stages within one file. Approval gates attach to Environment resources, so the production stage waits for the designated approvers before running. The entire delivery flow is versioned alongside the source code and observable as a single run. Classic release pipelines are legacy, deprecated for new work, and split build and release across two products that don't share approval policy in one place. A runtime parameter can gate execution but lacks the per-environment audit trail and reviewer permissions that an environment approval gives you. Chaining three pipelines fragments observability and reruns across three places and still needs an approval mechanism bolted on at the production pipeline.
questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines

questions.question: A pipeline must deploy resources to an Azure subscription that is reachable only from a private network behind a corporate firewall. Microsoft-hosted agents cannot reach the target. What is the correct approach?
options: Whitelist the Microsoft-hosted agent IP ranges on the corporate firewall so the agent can reach the private target subscription
Use the AzureCLI@2 task with a service connection scoped to a managed identity holding Reader permissions on the firewall and on the destination Azure subscription
Move the pipeline to GitHub Actions and use a runner group with the private-network label, which Azure DevOps tasks recognise as an in-network execution context
Deploy a self-hosted agent inside the private network and configure the pipeline pool to target that agent's pool so jobs run from inside the network perimeter
questions.explanation: Self-hosted agents run on machines you operate, so an agent placed inside the private network has direct line-of-sight to in-network resources; the pipeline routes jobs to it via the agent pool name. Whitelisting Microsoft-hosted agent ranges is explicitly discouraged because the ranges are large and rotate weekly with the Azure IP service tags. A service connection controls how the pipeline authenticates to Azure ARM, not how the underlying job reaches the network — Reader on the firewall does not punch a hole through it. A GitHub Actions runner group lives in the Actions runner pool and is not addressable from an Azure DevOps pool, and the 'private-network' label is not a special directive that opens any path either.

questions.question: A pipeline applies Terraform to provision Azure infrastructure. State must be shared across parallel runs without conflicting writes. Which configuration provides this safely?
options: A local state file committed to the same repository as the Terraform code so every pipeline run pulls the latest version with the source
An Azure Storage account backend with a blob container holding the state file, where the azurerm backend takes a blob lease to serialise concurrent writes
An Azure Key Vault secret named terraform-state holding the serialised state JSON, retrieved at the start of each run and written back at completion
Separate state files per pipeline run, each named with the build number, then merged together by a custom step at the end of the workflow to form one state
questions.explanation: The azurerm remote backend stores state in an Azure Storage blob and acquires a blob lease as an exclusive lock during operations, so parallel runs wait for the lease rather than tearing each other's writes. A local state file in Git has no locking at all — two pipeline runs racing to commit produce merge conflicts, and the state file itself records resource attributes (including secrets) in plaintext that should never live in source control. Key Vault is designed for small immutable secrets and is the wrong shape for the multi-megabyte mutable JSON Terraform produces; it has no provider integration and no per-operation locking. Per-run state files fundamentally break Terraform because the tool identifies and reconciles resources by a single authoritative state — merging multiple states programmatically is not supported and will desynchronise the recorded resources from reality.

questions.question: A pipeline needs the database connection string for a production deployment. The value must not appear in pipeline logs and must rotate without editing the YAML. Which mechanism is best?
options: Store the value in a pipeline parameter of type secret and supply it manually at queue time so operators paste the value into the dialog on each run
Encode the connection string as base64 and place it in a pipeline variable marked secret, then decode the value inside the deployment task at runtime each run
Commit the connection string to the repository in an encrypted file and use a custom decryption task that pulls the key material from runner environment variables
Reference the value from an Azure Key Vault using a variable group linked to that vault, with the pipeline's service principal granted Get permission on secrets
questions.explanation: A variable group linked to Azure Key Vault resolves the secret at run time, so rotating the value in the vault takes effect on the next run with no YAML edit, and Azure Pipelines automatically masks any matching string in the log output. Pipeline parameters do not have a secret type, and manual entry blocks unattended automation and is trivially leaked through shoulder-surfing or pasted into the wrong dialog. Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone with log access who notices an unmasked base64 string can decode it, and the value still has to be rotated by editing the pipeline. Committing an encrypted blob shifts the problem to distributing the decryption key, which then has to live somewhere — typically as an environment variable — recreating exactly the secret-sprawl Key Vault is meant to solve.
questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan

questions.question: A pipeline builds a Docker image and pushes it to Azure Container Registry. The same image must be deployed unchanged to dev, staging, and production. Which tagging approach supports reliable promotion across environments?
options: Tag the image as latest and configure each environment's deployment to pull image:latest at container startup
Tag the image with both an immutable identifier such as the build number or commit SHA and a moving tag for convenience, deploying environments by the immutable tag
Build a separate image per environment using environment-specific Dockerfiles, tagged myapp:dev, myapp:staging, and myapp:prod, for clear separation of build contexts
Tag the image with the environment name at build time and overwrite the staging and production tags during deployment so each environment shows its current build
questions.explanation: Immutable tags such as a commit SHA or build ID guarantee that the exact artifact promoted from dev is what runs in production, which is the build-once-deploy-many invariant. The latest tag is mutable and racy: between pulls in different environments it can refer to different digests, so you cannot prove that staging and production ran the same bits. Per-environment Dockerfiles defeat the build-once principle outright — dev now ships different code paths than prod, which is precisely what the practice is meant to prevent. Overwriting environment-named tags during deployment makes rollbacks ambiguous because the meaning of myapp:prod changes over time, so 'redeploy the previous prod tag' no longer identifies a specific image.

questions.question: A web application has been instrumented with Application Insights. The team wants to be alerted within minutes if the 95th-percentile response time exceeds 800 ms for a sustained period. What is the correct configuration?
options: A log query alert that runs traces | where severityLevel == 3 every minute and pages the on-call team whenever any matching trace record is found in the workspace
An Application Insights smart detection rule that automatically learns the baseline and fires when the failed-request rate doubles compared to the prior calendar week
An Azure Function timer trigger that polls the Application Insights REST API hourly and emails a report of slow requests recorded during the preceding one-hour window
An Azure Monitor metric alert against the requests/duration metric using the P95 aggregation, evaluated over a 5-minute window with the threshold set to 800 ms
questions.explanation: Application Insights publishes request duration as a metric that supports percentile aggregations, so a metric alert over requests/duration with the P95 aggregation and an 800 ms threshold matches the requirement directly and fires within minutes. A trace log query keyed on severityLevel measures error severity, not latency percentiles, so it would never catch a slow-but-successful request. Smart detection targets failure-rate anomalies against a learned baseline; it does not let you set a hard latency threshold like 800 ms. Polling the REST API hourly from a Function adds the polling interval as fixed latency, so an incident can run for nearly an hour before the report is sent — well past the 'within minutes' requirement.

questions.question: A team wants to release a new checkout flow gradually, starting with 5 percent of users and increasing to 100 percent over a week, with the ability to roll the change back instantly. Which approach best supports this?
options: Deploy two versions of the application to separate App Services and shift traffic between them using Azure Front Door weighted routing rules updated manually each day
Maintain two long-running release branches in source control and deploy whichever branch matches the current rollout state, rebuilding the application for each step
Use Azure App Configuration feature flags with a targeting filter that gates rollout percentage, toggled via the portal or API with no application redeploy required
Read the rollout percentage from an environment variable set at App Service startup and restart the App Service whenever the percentage value is changed during the rollout
questions.explanation: Feature flags decouple deployment from release. Azure App Configuration provides feature flags with built-in percentage and targeting filters that the application evaluates per request, so the rollout percentage changes instantly from the portal or API with no redeploy and no restart, and rollback is the same toggle in reverse. Front Door weighted routing balances traffic between two whole deployments but it does not address per-user feature exposure — every user on the new deployment sees every change in that build, so you cannot turn just the checkout flow back off. Branch-based gating forces a rebuild for every percentage change and conflates code state with rollout state, so rollback means rebuilding and redeploying instead of flipping a switch. Restarting the App Service to change an env var causes a brief outage each step and still cannot target a specific user subset.
questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications

questions.question: A pipeline must guarantee that no Azure resource is deployed without required tags and that storage accounts always have HTTPS-only enabled, regardless of which pipeline performs the deployment. What is the most robust enforcement?
options: Author Azure Policy definitions assigned at the subscription or management-group scope that deny deployments missing the required tags or the HTTPS-only storage configuration
Add an Azure Resource Manager template validation step to every pipeline that fails the build whenever required tags or HTTPS-only settings are missing from the template
Configure branch policies on the infrastructure repository that require a security-team reviewer for any pull request touching storage account or tag-related YAML or Bicep files
Use a self-hosted agent pool whose startup script scans the resource graph nightly and emails a non-compliance report listing resources without tags or with HTTPS-only disabled
questions.explanation: Azure Policy enforces the requirement at the Azure Resource Manager control plane. A deny policy assigned at the subscription or management-group scope blocks any deployment that violates the rule, regardless of which pipeline, ARM template, Bicep file, Terraform run, or portal click attempted it — the platform is the gate, not the tool. Template validation in one pipeline only enforces against deployments that flow through that pipeline; another pipeline, a portal user, or a CLI script bypasses it entirely. Branch policies depend on every deployment originating from that repository, which is also bypassed by anything outside the repo. Nightly scans detect drift after the fact rather than preventing it, so non-compliant resources can run for up to 24 hours before being noticed.
questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan

questions.question: A YAML pipeline must authenticate to Azure to deploy resources, and the security team forbids storing any client secret or certificate for the service connection. Which Azure DevOps service connection authentication type meets this requirement?
options: A service principal (manual) connection whose client secret is stored in a secret pipeline variable and rotated every 90 days by an automated job
A workload identity federation service connection that uses OpenID Connect to obtain short-lived Azure tokens with no stored secret
A managed identity connection that embeds the identity's primary access key in the connection definition for the pipeline to read
A personal access token connection scoped to the deploying user's Azure role assignments and refreshed at each pipeline run
questions.explanation: Workload identity federation configures an Azure service connection to exchange a pipeline-issued OIDC token for a short-lived Azure access token, so no client secret or certificate is ever stored — the trust relationship is the credential. A service principal (manual) connection still keeps a client secret in the connection (even if also mirrored to a pipeline variable), which is exactly what is forbidden. Managed identities do not expose a retrievable 'primary access key' that you embed somewhere; the wording confuses managed identities with storage account access keys, and embedding a key would itself violate the rule. Personal access tokens authenticate to Azure DevOps itself, not to Azure resources, and a PAT is still a long-lived stored credential, so it fails on both counts.
questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan

questions.question: A team wants pull requests to main to automatically associate with the work items they implement, so traceability reports show which requirements shipped. Which Azure Repos configuration enforces that every completed PR is linked to at least one work item?
options: A branch policy on main that enables the Check for linked work items requirement as a blocking policy
A pipeline task that parses the commit message for an AB# token and fails the build when none is present
A repository-level setting that automatically creates a placeholder work item for every pull request opened
An Azure Boards query saved as a dashboard widget that lists pull requests missing a work item link
questions.explanation: The Check for linked work items branch policy on main can be set to required (blocking), so a pull request cannot complete unless it links at least one work item, which gives traceability at the merge gate. Parsing commit messages for an AB# token in a pipeline only runs after the build kicks off and produces a build failure rather than blocking the PR completion button, and developers can amend or work around the parser. Auto-creating placeholder work items produces meaningless links to empty stubs rather than tying PRs to real requirements, defeating the point of the report. A Boards query widget surfaces missing links after the fact for someone to chase, but it enforces nothing at the moment the PR is completed.
questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy

questions.question: A monolithic repository takes a long time to clone on Microsoft-hosted agents because of a large history of binary assets, slowing every CI run. Which combination most directly reduces clone time on each pipeline run?
options: Enable shallow fetch with a small fetch depth on the pipeline checkout and migrate large binaries to Git LFS
Increase the agent job timeout and add more parallel jobs so the long clone overlaps with other build stages
Switch the repository from Git to Team Foundation Version Control so only the latest changeset is downloaded
Schedule the CI pipeline to run less frequently so the cumulative clone cost across the day is reduced
questions.explanation: Shallow fetch caps how much history the checkout downloads (--depth 1 grabs only the tip commit), and migrating large binaries to Git LFS keeps the blobs out of the working clone altogether, so each run fetches a fraction of the data. Raising the timeout and parallelising jobs hides the cost rather than reducing it — the clone still has to finish before the build can start. Switching to TFVC is a disruptive change of source control system that Microsoft positions Git as the preferred option over, and it does not address the binary-history root cause cleanly. Reducing CI frequency degrades developer feedback without making any individual clone faster.
questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy

questions.question: A release must not proceed to the production stage until an Azure Monitor query confirms that error rates in the canary remain below a threshold for 10 minutes after the canary deploy. Which Azure Pipelines environment check provides this automated quality verification?
options: A required reviewers approval check assigned to the on-call engineer who must approve the production environment manually
A business hours check that delays the production stage until the next maintenance window opens for the production environment
A Query Azure Monitor alerts check on the environment that evaluates alert state before allowing the stage
An exclusive lock check that prevents concurrent runs from deploying to the environment simultaneously during a release
questions.explanation: The Query Azure Monitor alerts environment check polls Azure Monitor and only lets the stage proceed when no matching alert is firing, which is the native way to automate a canary health gate end-to-end. A required reviewers check adds a human approval but evaluates no telemetry, so the on-call engineer is the one who has to look at the dashboard manually. A business hours check only restricts when deployments may run, not whether the canary is healthy — error rates can still spike during business hours. An exclusive lock serialises concurrent runs on the same environment but says nothing about error rates or canary health, so a broken canary still proceeds as long as nothing else is running.
questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines

questions.question: A team adopting OpenTelemetry wants distributed traces from a .NET microservice to flow into Application Insights so end-to-end request correlation appears in the Application Map. What is the recommended integration?
options: Add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro to the service and configure it with the Application Insights connection string
Write a nightly export job that copies OpenTelemetry spans from local files into the Application Insights REST API
Enable IIS request logging on the host and forward the W3C logs to a Log Analytics custom table
Install a third-party tracing backend and screen-scrape its dashboards into an Application Insights workbook for visualisation
questions.explanation: The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro is the supported path: adding the NuGet package and supplying the Application Insights connection string streams traces with full span context to Application Insights, which is what populates the Application Map with end-to-end correlation. A nightly export job batches spans hours behind real time, losing the live correlation view and creating a latency gap during incidents. IIS request logging captures coarse web-server access logs without span IDs, so it cannot reconstruct a distributed call graph across services. A third-party backend behind screen-scraped dashboards never feeds structured trace telemetry into Application Insights, so the Application Map stays empty.

questions.question: A pipeline publishes an internal NuGet package consumed by several teams. Consumers must always resolve dependencies through a single feed that proxies and caches public packages while also hosting the internal one. Which Azure Artifacts capability provides this?
options: Publish the package to a public NuGet.org account and have consumers add it as a second package source
An Azure Artifacts feed with an upstream source to nuget.org so it both hosts internal packages and proxies public ones
A pipeline artifact attached to each build that consumers download and reference by local file path
A universal package stored in the feed and extracted by each consumer with the az artifacts CLI as a pre-build restore step
questions.explanation: An Azure Artifacts feed with an upstream source pointing at nuget.org serves the internal package directly and transparently proxies and caches public packages, so consumers configure one nuget.config source and dependency resolution flows through it for both. Publishing the package on NuGet.org exposes private code publicly and still leaves consumers configuring two sources rather than one. Pipeline artifacts are build outputs referenced by file path on the agent; they are not a managed package feed with version resolution, restore caching, or transitive dependency handling. Universal packages store arbitrary files outside the NuGet protocol and are not consumed through nuget restore, so they cannot satisfy a NuGet dependency reference at build time.
